The papers you've provided don't test sodium-based electrolytes in lithium-ion cells, so they can't answer this directly. They do show what each chemistry's electrolyte looks like and why they differ.

**What the papers show**

- **Sodium electrolytes:** Sodium cells in these papers use NaPF6 salts. One uses NaPF6 in tetraglyme (Carter et al., Nano Lett. 2017, p. 3), and another uses 1 M NaPF6 in diglyme (Cohn et al., Nano Lett. 2017, p. 2). The authors chose glyme solvents because they form stable interfaces on sodium metal, whereas carbonate electrolytes do not (Cohn et al., p. 1).
- **Lithium electrolytes:** The lithium-ion cells use different salts and solvents. One uses 1.2 M LiPF6 in EC/EMC (Bai/Muralidharan et al., Adv. Mater. 2020, p. 12), and another uses 1 M LiClO4 in propylene carbonate (Muralidharan et al., ACS Nano 2017, p. 6).
- **Why they differ:** Sodium ions have a larger ionic radius and a less negative standard reduction potential than lithium ions (Cohn et al., p. 1). Sodium metal is also less stable in carbonate electrolytes than lithium metal (Cohn et al., p. 1).

**What I can't confirm from these papers**

A lithium-ion cell needs Li⁺ in the electrolyte to shuttle lithium between electrodes. If the electrolyte contained only Na⁺, the cell would have no lithium to cycle, unless the electrodes were already loaded with sodium. The sodium cells in these papers avoid that issue by pre-sodiating the cathode (Cohn et al., p. 4). Whether mixed Li/Na electrolytes work in a lithium cell is not addressed in any of the documents.

This is general electrochemical reasoning, not something the papers establish. For a definitive answer, you would need a source that specifically tests sodium salts in lithium cells.
